projects.title: LIFT Tracker (Land Inventory Fast Track)
projects.description: Interactive map unveiled July 30, 2026 tracking New York City's pipeline of affordable housing planned for publicly owned land. It covers more than 100 city-owned sites across the five boroughs where more than 50,000 homes are slated to be built, showing housing alongside the libraries and community space going up with it. Mayor Zohran Mamdani framed the launch as making clear that city-owned land is not sitting idle. It sits inside the administration's Block by Block program, which targets 200,000 new affordable units and 200,000 preserved ones over ten years, against a budget of $22 billion for affordable housing over five years, with nearly $5 billion for new construction in the first two.
projects.why_interesting: The city has never published a running, site-level ledger of what it intends to build on its own land. Putting the pipeline on a public map converts a political promise into something checkable parcel by parcel, which is the only way a ten-year housing target ever gets audited.

projects.title: NYC Council Vision Zero interactive map
projects.description: Public map released August 5, 2026 letting residents search how intersections in their own neighborhoods were treated under Vision Zero, paired with the Council Data Team's analysis of which treatments actually reduced harm. The study examined nearly 10,000 intersections that received interventions between 2015 and 2021, comparing pedestrian casualty data from 2013 through 2023. Turn traffic calming cut pedestrian casualties 27 percent, neighborhood slow zones 21 percent, leading pedestrian intervals 13 percent and the citywide speed limit reduction 10 percent. Speaker Julie Menin presented it as evidence of which street-safety strategies work best.
projects.why_interesting: Vision Zero has run for more than a decade on the assumption that its toolkit works without ranking the tools against each other. Attaching an effect size to each treatment type, then letting a resident look up their own corner, turns a citywide slogan into a procurement argument.

projects.title: NYC Legislation Implementation Tracker
projects.description: Tal Roded's tracker (NYCuriosity) reads the text of enacted New York City local laws and extracts every duty they impose on city agencies. It covers laws enacted from 2014 through July 2026, pulling more than 5,000 agency obligations out of over 800 local laws across more than 60 agencies, and flags deadlines falling in the next twelve months. Five views drive it: a searchable obligations table, a bar chart ranking agencies by obligation burden and deliverable type (rules, reports, programs, outreach), a timeline covering past-due and recurring items, a per-law implementation checklist and a methodology page. Source legislation comes from NYC Legistar; agency names are normalized against the city's Agencies and Governance Organizations dataset. Every quoted passage is mechanically verified against the original law text. Its framing: every new local law is a to-do list for city agencies.
projects.why_interesting: The gap between passing a law and doing what it says is where most city accountability reporting dies, because nobody maintains the list of what was actually required. Building that list mechanically, with verbatim quotes checked against statute, produces the denominator that oversight hearings have always lacked.

projects.title: subway.fyi
projects.description: Real-time subway instrument built on the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's GTFS-Realtime feeds, surfaced in BetaNYC's August 13 roundup as a reader-built explorable dataset. Its live map animates every train along its actual track, refreshing every five seconds. An awfulness map color-codes every station by current wait time and bunching, updating each minute. A delay radar detects unusual gaps between trains and fires a prediction when the live pattern matches shapes that historically preceded official Metropolitan Transportation Authority delay alerts.
projects.why_interesting: Most transit dashboards report yesterday's on-time percentage. Scoring stations on bunching right now, and predicting the delay alert before the agency issues it, treats the realtime feed as a leading indicator rather than a record -- and the awfulness framing is an editorial choice that makes the data legible to riders instead of planners.

projects.title: Manhattan Rent Stabilization Explorer
projects.description: Alihan Polat's (Polat Planning and Analytics) tax-lot-level map of Manhattan's rent-stabilized housing stock, covering 2008 through 2025 with a timeline slider that shows how individual properties' stabilization status changed year by year. Lots fall into three classes: units currently registered as rent stabilized, lots previously stabilized with no current units but a historical record, and other residential lots with no recorded stabilized units through the selected year. Aggregate Manhattan counters report total residential units, stabilized units, the stabilized share and residential tax-lot counts. Featured in BetaNYC's July 30 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Stabilized-unit loss is usually argued at the borough level, where it is a single shrinking number. Rendering it lot by lot across seventeen years turns deregulation into a geography with an address attached, and the previously stabilized category is the one that shows where the stock actually went.

projects.title: NYC Municipal Archives: Neighborhood Stories map
projects.description: Interactive map from the New York City Department of Records and Information Services linking resident-submitted oral histories to the places they describe, across all five boroughs. Each point on the map is one personal interview about a neighborhood, a memory or a moment in city life, and the project is actively collecting more. Surfaced in BetaNYC's July 30 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: The archives normally hold the city's official record of itself. Geocoding first-person interviews against that same map puts resident memory into the same index as the property cards and permits, which is a quiet argument about what counts as a municipal record.

projects.title: Building Indicator Project: 20th lender roundtable
projects.description: The University Neighborhood Housing Program's Building Indicator Project scores New York City multifamily properties for physical and financial distress, tracking more than 120 data points across over 70,000 rental buildings, with more than a decade of accumulated history and a scoring method built with lenders, advocates, property managers and researchers. Findings were presented August 5, 2026 at the project's 20th annual multifamily lender roundtable, attended by more than 50 representatives from 16 multifamily lenders. Two figures anchored the meeting: Bronx median price per unit fell from $175,000 in 2018 to $96,000 in 2025, and insurance costs rose from roughly $800 per unit in 2019 to nearly $2,000 per unit by 2026.
projects.why_interesting: A distress index that lenders themselves show up to read once a year is a rare thing -- the data has an actual audience with money at stake. The Bronx price collapse next to the insurance line is the clearest available statement of why the outer-borough multifamily math stopped working.

projects.title: NYC Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crew
projects.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Chief Technology Officer and Office of Technology and Innovation Commissioner Lisa Gelobter launched the PIT Crew on July 13, 2026: five in-house teams of product managers, designers, engineers, user researchers and data experts embedded alongside city agencies to build digital public goods rather than procure them. Some 2,800 people applied; the administration plans to hire 30 full-time staff across four crews using $5.24 million in baselined city funding, with a fifth team supported by the Rockefeller Foundation through the Mayor's Fund to Advance New York City. The first crew works with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection on a portal for filing complaints about hard-to-cancel subscriptions, backing the city's Click to Cancel protections. BetaNYC ran an August 12 BetaBagels session to meet the crew, and it stayed a lead item through the August 7 and August 13 roundups.
projects.why_interesting: The build-versus-buy question is the one that determines whether any of this data infrastructure survives an administration change, and 2,800 applicants for 30 jobs is a real answer to the claim that government cannot recruit technologists. Worth watching as a template other cities copy or fail to.

projects.title: Anniston Transparency Portal
projects.description: Anniston, Alabama launched a consolidated transparency portal on August 4, 2026, pulling dashboards from across city departments into one mobile-friendly place. It covers the adopted budget, revenue and expenditures, department spending and capital investments; a capital projects dashboard organized by budget, reported spending, remaining balance, funding category and status; City Clerk records including public records activity, claims administration and pension fund information; Police and Fire Department statistics with calls for service and crime categories; building and safety inspection records by result, month and category with personal identifying information stripped; Community Development Block Grant and HOME program detail; permits, construction activity and business licenses; Main Street Anniston and Museums and Gardens program data; and online work orders and code violation reports.
projects.why_interesting: A city of roughly 20,000 shipping a portal this broad is the more interesting version of the open data story -- the tooling has gotten cheap enough that transparency infrastructure is no longer restricted to cities with a data team. The capital projects view, with remaining balance exposed, is the part big cities usually refuse to publish.

projects.title: Palm Springs GIS Maps and Data Portal
projects.description: Palm Springs, California opened a geographic information system maps and data portal on July 23, 2026, built for phones and tablets as much as desktops. Residents can look up their City Council district, pull zoning and property information, check the status of street and pavement improvement projects and find nearby parks, trails, bikeways and public art installations.
projects.why_interesting: The pavement-project layer is the tell: routing capital-works status into the same lookup as zoning and districts is how a portal stops being a data catalog and starts answering the question residents actually arrive with, which is when my street gets fixed.

projects.title: NYC Council: history_map
projects.description: Repository created August 12, 2026 by the New York City Council Data Team for viewing census demographic information from 1940 through 2020. Described by its author, Noah, as made mostly for fun. Pushed to the same day it was created.
projects.why_interesting: Eighty years of census demographics on one map is a serious spine for any neighborhood-change argument, and the fact that it shows up as a Council staffer's side project is a decent indicator of where that team's tooling has gotten to. Early, but worth tracking to see whether it graduates into a published tool.

projects.title: NYC Council: 9/11 memorials and street co-namings map
projects.description: New York City Council Data Team repository created July 20, 2026 and pushed through July 31, mapping September 11-related street co-namings and memorials across the city, prepared for the twenty-fifth anniversary on September 11, 2026.
projects.why_interesting: Street co-namings are one of the few civic records that mark grief geographically, and they have never been assembled as a single memorial layer. Built ahead of the twenty-fifth anniversary, it is also a useful example of a data team working to an editorial calendar.

projects.title: NYC Council: vision-zero-final analysis repository
projects.description: The New York City Council Data Team's Vision Zero analysis repository, holding the code behind the August 5, 2026 public map and the intersection-level effectiveness findings on roughly 10,000 treated intersections. Published alongside vision-zero-web, the Quarto site that renders the public-facing version.
projects.why_interesting: Publishing the analysis code next to the finished map is what separates a legislative body making a claim from one inviting a check on it. Anyone disputing the 27 percent turn-calming figure can now go read how it was computed.
